42878795.label: Purpose
42878795.text: To determine whether sequential fluoroscopic defecography (FLD) and MR defecography (MRD) change clinical management of patients with pelvic floor dysfunction and to identify factors associated with management change.

42878795.label: Methods
42878795.text: Multi-institutional retrospective study including adults who underwent both FL and MR defecography within 3 years, without interval surgery. Primary outcome was management change attributed to the second examination. Clinical information, test order & timing, multidisciplinary review, and imaging variables were compared between patients with and without management change. Univariate analyses were performed overall and by first-modality subgroup. Multivariable logistic regression was performed in the overall cohort.

42878795.label: Results
42878795.text: Of 46 patients, 24 underwent FLD first and 22 underwent MRD first. Management changed after second examination in 23.9% (11/46). FLD-first order (adjusted OR, 72.70; 95% CI, 2.77-1909.81; p = 0.010), shorter interval between examinations (adjusted OR per 30 days, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.68-1.00; p = 0.038), and wider MR resting anorectal angle (adjusted OR per degree, 1.10; 95% CI, 1.02-1.20; p = 0.016) were independent predictors of management change. MRD after FLD showed more frequent new second-test abnormalities than FLD after MRD (16/24 [66.7%] vs. 5/22 [22.7%], p = 0.0037), particularly new cystocele detection (41.7% vs. 0%, p = 0.0006). In the FLD-first subgroup, multidisciplinary review was associated with management change (5/5 [100%] vs. 5/19 [26.3%], p = 0.0059).

42878795.label: Conclusion
42878795.text: Sequential multimodality defecography changed management in approximately one-quarter of patients. Its value was greatest when MRD followed FLD, especially when examinations were performed closely together. MRD after FLD detected a higher frequency of second-test abnormalities, particularly cystocele. The association between multidisciplinary review and management change suggests that the clinical impact of sequential defecography depends not only on the added imaging findings but also on how they are integrated into treatment planning.

42879295.text: There are numerous terms used to describe variant locations of intrauterine devices (IUDs) in US reports, such as displaced, low lying, and malpositioned. These vague terms are frequently misinterpreted by providers and patients, which may lead to an incorrect inference of inadequate contraception. Current consensus guidelines from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) indicate that the greatest risk of unintended pregnancy may be due to the unnecessary removal of a nonfundal IUD. Many providers now advocate leaving an IUD in place if it is located entirely above the internal os, as the device still provides effective contraception. The ACOG recommends counseling for patients, whether symptomatic or asymptomatic, before removal of the IUD. The authors outline a simple lexicon to describe the location of IUDs in US reports that includes terms understood by obstetrics and gynecology providers and that better align with current gynecologic literature.

42911395.label: Purpose
42911395.text: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of percentage signal intensity (SI) drop on chemical-shift magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for distinguishing Fuhrman grade 1 from Fuhrman grades 2-4 clear-cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC).

42911395.label: Methods
42911395.text: This retrospective multicenter study included 85 patients with histopathologically confirmed ccRCC who underwent preoperative 1.5-T MRI including chemical-shift sequences between 2016 and 2024. Percentage tumour-to-spleen SI drop was calculated from in-phase and opposed-phase images. Tumours were classified as Fuhrman grade 1 (n = 30) or Fuhrman grades 2-4 (n = 55), based on grades recorded in the original surgical pathology reports. MRI findings were compared between groups, and ROC curve analysis was performed to evaluate the discriminatory performance of percentage SI drop.

42911395.label: Results
42911395.text: Percentage SI drop was significantly greater in Fuhrman grade 1 tumours than in Fuhrman grades 2-4 tumours [40.0% (IQR, 25.4-54.2) vs. 17.4% (IQR, 5.9-29.2); p = 0.003]. Fuhrman grades 2-4 tumours were significantly larger than grade 1 tumours [46 mm (IQR, 28-74) vs. 39 mm (IQR, 30-49); p = 0.01], whereas tumour composition did not differ significantly (p = 0.08). ROC analysis showed modest discriminatory performance (AUC, 0.695; 95% CI, 0.566-0.824; p = 0.003). A percentage SI drop cut-off of ≥ 27.8% yielded 66.7% sensitivity and 67.3% specificity for identifying Fuhrman grade 1 tumours.

42911395.label: Conclusion
42911395.text: Percentage SI drop was greater in Fuhrman grade 1 than in Fuhrman grades 2-4 ccRCCs, but discrimination was modest and incremental value beyond tumour size was not established. These findings are limited to an exploratory comparison using historical Fuhrman grades and cannot be extrapolated to contemporary World Health Organization/International Society of Urological Pathology (WHO/ISUP) grading.

42980945.label: Objective
42980945.text: To evaluate the real-world diagnostic performance of PI-RADS for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) across large-scale worldwide cohorts.

42980945.label: Materials and methods
42980945.text: This multicenter observational study included 20,429 patients from nine Chinese institutions and a published worldwide meta-analysis dataset comprising 13,330 patients for comparison. All PI-RADS assessments were extracted from original MRI reports produced by clinical radiologists as part of standard diagnostic workflows. Summary receiver operating characteristic curves were constructed using a bivariate random-effects model, and center-level areas under the curve (AUCs) were pooled via random-effects meta-analysis. Subgroup analyses were conducted.

42980945.label: Results
42980945.text: PI-RADS exhibited overall discriminatory performance for csPCa across nine Chinese cohorts comparable to the META results from 70 studies, though significant inter-center variation was observed. Using a PI-RADS ≥ 3 threshold, pooled sensitivity was 92.6% and specificity was 51.5%. At a PI-RADS ≥ 4 threshold, pooled specificity improved to 78.1%, with a sensitivity of 81.5%. The overall diagnostic performance was consistent across thresholds: The summary ROC (SROC) AUC was 0.903 for PI-RADS ≥ 3 and 0.826 for PI-RADS ≥ 4 in detecting csPCa at the meta-analysis level. Subgroup analyses indicated better performance among older patients (≥ 70 years) and those with higher PSA levels (> 20 ng/mL). PI-RADS v2.1 outperformed v2 or earlier versions in most clinical scenarios.

42980945.label: Conclusions
42980945.text: This large-scale real-world study provides critical multicenter evidence supporting the use of PI-RADS in clinical practice worldwide, while also revealing substantial variability in scoring and diagnostic performance across institutions. The findings offer an evidence-based overview of PI-RADS implementation in China and worldwide, highlighting both its utility and inconsistencies.

42980945.label: Key points
42980945.text: Question What are the real-world PI-RADS diagnostic performance benchmarks for clinically significant prostate cancer detection across diverse Chinese multicenter institutions versus global data? Findings PI-RADS demonstrated good overall performance (SROC AUC 0.903 at a threshold of ≥ 3), with superior discriminatory ability in older patients, higher PSA levels, and v2.1 users. Critical relevance statement This article critically assesses substantial inter-institutional heterogeneity in PI-RADS performance, highlighting that pooled estimates should not replace local calibration and that regionally adapted implementation strategies are essential for advancing clinical radiology practice.

42998145.label: Objectives
42998145.text: Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is central to bladder cancer assessment with the Vesical Imaging-Reporting and Data System (VI-RADS). Computed diffusion-weighted imaging (cDWI) reduces scan time but has limited signal-to-noise ratio (SNR); its voxelwise variant, voxelwise-computed diffusion-weighted imaging (vcDWI), may overcome this limitation. We evaluated whether vcDWI provides better image quality and shorter interpretation time while maintaining diagnostic accuracy compared with acquired DWI (aDWI) in VI-RADS assessment.

42998145.label: Methods
42998145.text: This single-center study included 111 consecutive patients with bladder cancer who underwent magnetic resonance imaging between October 2019 and October 2024. Two radiologists (2 and 5 years' experience) assessed image quality and objective metrics: tumor SNR (SNRtumor), urine-referenced SNR, contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and urine-referenced contrast ratio (CR, the ratio of tumor to urine signal intensity); they performed VI-RADS scoring and recorded interpretation times. Diagnostic performance for muscle invasion (VI-RADS ≥ 4) was evaluated against histopathology.

42998145.label: Results
42998145.text: vcDWI showed higher urine-referenced SNR and contrast ratio than all aDWI sequences (all p < 0.001), with CNR comparable to b = 1400 s/mm², whereas lesion-only SNRtumor was lower than at b = 700 and b = 1400 s/mm². It received superior subjective scores for lesion clarity and overall image quality (all p < 0.001). Diagnostic performance was comparable, with the difference in area under the curve (AUC) within a 0.10 non-inferiority margin in an exploratory post hoc analysis (AUCs, vcDWI vs. aDWI: 0.86 vs. 0.85 and 0.90 vs. 0.91; one-sided 95% upper bounds 0.030 and 0.054). vcDWI reduced interpretation time (median times 16.0% and 28.6% lower; p < 0.001), and inter-observer agreement was good for aDWI and excellent for vcDWI (weighted κ = 0.797 vs. 0.895).

42998145.label: Conclusions
42998145.text: vcDWI improved tumor conspicuity and background suppression, was compatible with non-inferiority to aDWI in an exploratory analysis, and reduced interpretation time in VI-RADS assessment, with good-to-excellent inter-observer agreement.

43055695.text: Chronic liver disease, caused by a range of etiologies, can lead to progressive liver function deterioration, hepatic fibrosis, cirrhosis, and, ultimately, end-stage liver disease. With cirrhosis and end-stage liver disease, complications include portal hypertension, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, refractory ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, and primary hepatocellular carcinoma. Imaging plays an important role in the diagnosis, treatment response assessment, and surveillance of chronic liver disease, specifically of hepatic hemochromatosis, steatosis, and fibrosis, in an effort to prevent progression to cirrhosis. This document reviews the imaging modalities best suited for these clinical scenarios, and a summary of current evidence is provided to support the use of various modalities for each of the clinical contexts. The American College of Radiology Appropriateness Criteria are evidence-based guidelines for specific clinical conditions that are reviewed annually by a multidisciplinary expert panel. The guideline development and revision include an extensive analysis of current medical literature from peer reviewed journals and the application of well-established methodologies (RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method and Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation or GRADE) to rate the appropriateness of imaging and treatment procedures for specific clinical scenarios. In those instances where evidence is lacking or equivocal, expert opinion may supplement the available evidence to recommend imaging or treatment.

43079095.text: A 33-year-old woman presented with long-standing abdominal distension and unexplained ascites. Serum CA125 levels were significantly elevated. Abdominal CT revealed a cystic lesion in the left adnexal region with massive ascites. To determine the etiology, 18F-FDG PET/CT was performed after fasting for at least 6 h. The adnexal lesion showed no appreciable FDG uptake, favoring a benign cystic lesion. Unexpectedly,​ heterogeneous hypermetabolism was found along the right heart border. Because the interpretation of cardiac FDG findings may be confounded by physiological or nonspecific myocardial uptake, ¹⁸F-FAPI PET/CT was subsequently performed for further characterization, which revealed a more extensive and conspicuous tracer uptake within the cardiac lesion than FDG PET/CT, more clearly delineating its extent. The patient subsequently underwent partial surgical resection of the cardiac mass with biopsy. Histomorphological, immunohistochemical, and molecular findings supported the diagnosis of cardiac spindle cell sarcoma with partial myofibroblastic differentiation. This case reports a rare primary cardiac spindle cell sarcoma and highlights the complementary value of FDG and FAPI PET/CT in evaluating primary cardiac malignancies. It also underscores the importance of multimodal imaging in guiding differential diagnosis and clinical management.
